title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
shortTitle: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
summary: Visual Basic and its derivatives give adversaries a scripting environment that already ships with Windows. Visual Basic for Applications is embedded in Microsoft Office and several third party products, so a document can carry a macro that runs when the file is opened, while VBScript is a default Windows scripting language that can also run inside HTML application pages served to older browsers. Payloads frequently arrive as spearphishing attachments, and the attacker may need to bypass the mark of the web protection that normally flags files downloaded from the internet before the macro is allowed to run. Visual Basic also reaches Component Object Model interfaces and native Windows programming interfaces, so a short script can create processes, move files and download content. Detection focuses on Office applications spawning unusual child processes, macro execution recorded in application and endpoint telemetry, script host processes started with encoded content or from temporary and user download directories, script files created in unusual locations, and documents whose origin contradicts where they were found. Knowing which documents legitimately carry macros is the key differentiator.

beginner.definition: Visual Basic is an older but still supported programming language from Microsoft. Two versions of it live inside everyday Windows software, namely macros in Office files and VBScript files. Attackers use both to make a file do something as soon as it opens. Often the user only has to open the file and allow content.
beginner.whyItMatters: Office documents travel through email every single day. A harmful macro can arrive inside a file that looks like normal paperwork. Windows already includes everything needed to run that code, so nothing extra is installed. A single click can start the whole chain of events. Warnings do exist, but users often click straight through them.
howItWorks: A document arrives as an email attachment that looks like a normal business file.
The document contains a macro, which is a small program stored inside the file itself.
When the user opens it and allows content, the macro code starts running.
The macro can download other files, start programs or change system settings.
VBScript files work in a similar way and can be started directly by Windows.
Attackers may remove file warnings so that the macro runs without any prompt.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where every flatmate leaves notes on the fridge. One note says to open the back door for the plumber tomorrow at nine. Everyone trusts notes on the fridge, because that is how the flat works. A stranger slips his own note onto the fridge. It says the side gate should be left unlocked and the spare key put under the mat. The flatmate on duty follows it, because it looks like every other note. Nothing was forced, and the door was opened from the inside.
takeaways: Office macros are programs, so opening a file can be the same as running one.
Windows already contains scripting tools, so very little must be installed.
Documents arriving from outside your organisation deserve extra caution.

objectives: Explain what macros and VBScript are and where they run on Windows.
Describe how a document attachment can lead to code execution.
Explain the purpose of file origin warnings and how they can be bypassed.
Identify endpoint and Office telemetry that shows macro execution.
Describe why a baseline of legitimate macros improves detection.
